source_text: Ταῦτα ἡ πλάνη ἐπᾴδουσα ἔτι, καὶ τοιαῦτα συμβουλεύει· Τί πράττεις, ὦ οὗτος, καὶ οὐ τρυφᾷς, οὐδὲ ἐμφορῇ μὲν ἐδεσμάτων παντοίων, οἴνου δὲ ὑπερεμπίπλασαι; Οὐκ αἰσθάνῃ, ὡς ἐκ Θεοῦ ταυτὶ δέδοται πρὸς ἀπόλαυσιν ἀνεπικώλυτον; Περιβαλοῦ ἐσθῆτα νεόπλυτον, καὶ μύρῳ τὴν κεφαλὴν χρισάμενος, ὅρα τὴν γυναῖκα ταύτην, κἀκείνην δὲ ματαίως τὸν μάταιον πάρελθε βίον; Ἕτερον γὰρ οὐδὲν ὑπολείπεταί σοι παρὰ ταῦτα, οὐκ ἐνθάδε, οὐδὲ μετὰ θάνατον. Ἀλλὰ πράττε τὰ προστυχόντα. Οὔτε γὰρ λογισμὸν σέ τις τούτων εἰσπράξεται· οὔθ᾽ ὅλως γινώσκεται ἐκτὸς ἀνθρώπων τὰ ὑπ᾽ ἀνθρώπων γινόμενα. Ἅιδης δὲ, ὅ τί ποτε καὶ ἔστιν, εἰς ὃν ἀπιέναι λεγόμεθα, σοφίας καὶ αἰσθήσεως ἀμοιρεῖ. Ταῦτα μὲν οἱ μάταιοι.
thought_title: Error's advice: enjoy yourself, for nothing follows
orientation: Error, speaking in person, urges a life of pleasure because nothing follows death; Solomon calls this the talk of the vain.
pass_a_gloss: These things Error, still chanting as a spell, also advises such things: What are you doing, O you there, and not living luxuriously, nor filling yourself with all kinds of foods, and over-filling yourself with wine? Do you not perceive that these have been given from God for unhindered enjoyment? Put on fresh-washed clothing, and having anointed your head with perfume, look at this woman, and that one, and vainly pass through the vain life. For nothing else is left you besides these, not here, nor after death. But do the things that happen by. For neither will anyone exact an account of these from you; nor at all are the things done by men known outside of men. And Hades, whatever it is, into which we are said to depart, has no share of wisdom and perception. These things [say] the vain.

pass_b_english: Still chanting these spells, Error gives advice like this: "What are you doing, my man? Why are you not living in luxury, gorging yourself on every kind of food and filling yourself with wine beyond measure (Ecclesiastes 9:7)? Do you not see that these things have been given by God for enjoyment without hindrance? Put on freshly washed clothes, anoint your head with perfume, and look at this woman, and at that one, and pass your vain life in vain (Ecclesiastes 9:8-9). For nothing else is left to you besides these things, neither here nor after death. Rather, do whatever lies at hand (Ecclesiastes 9:10). For no one will demand from you an account of these things, and what human beings do is not known at all outside of human beings. And Hades, whatever it may be, where we are said to go, has no share in wisdom or perception (Ecclesiastes 9:10)." That is what the vain say.
notes: Numbering is the same in English and LXX. Voice: everything inside the quotation marks is the speech of Error (ἡ πλάνη) personified, closed by 'That is what the vain say'; it is not Gregory's teaching (source row note). The claim that these things are 'given by God for enjoyment' belongs to Error's speech. The print sets a Greek question mark after βίον, closing a run of imperatives; the English treats them as commands. 'Look at this woman, and at that one' renders ὅρα τὴν γυναῖκα ταύτην, κἀκείνην δέ, Gregory's turn on LXX 9:9 'see life with the wife whom you love'. 'Whatever lies at hand' renders τὰ προστυχόντα, echoing 9:10 'whatever your hand finds to do'. 'My man' renders ὦ οὗτος ('you there'). Hades is kept as the Greek name of the underworld.
